answer.rationale:
Only two memories have their archived source records in hand. exp_86 fully confirms memory_86: shortened onboarding lifted completion +13%, cut time-to-value 2.1 days, and — critically — improved 30-day retention +3%. That is the single direction with source-verified durable, not merely acquisition-shaped, benefit, so it is the defensible response to a price war: compete on realized value and time-to-value rather than on price.

The decisive finding is the gap between memory_73 and its source. The consolidated memory says targeted promotional pricing is 'effective ... with strong acquisition and revenue lift.' The source exp_73 shows signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, with the explicit conclusion that the discounted cohort does not survive first renewal and that discounting must NOT be generalized as sustainable growth. The consolidation silently dropped the harm and the do-not-generalize warning. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is disqualified: matching a competitor's deeper cut would buy a cohort that churns before renewal and would deepen, not stem, the SMB revenue problem. Meeting a price attack with price also concedes the frame permanently.

That single documented lossy consolidation is the reason I distrust the rest of the memory set rather than just the one entry. memory_31 (signup simplification / SMB activation), memory_57 (referral incentives, 'no measurable harm to retention'), memory_91 (activation messaging), and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) all read as clean, harm-free summaries in exactly the register memory_73 used before its source contradicted it. memory_57's explicit no-harm claim and memory_31's 'durable lift' are the phrasings I trust least, since memory_31 could easily be a partial restatement of the same onboarding work rather than independent evidence. None of these can be checked this cycle; they should be first in the queue next week.

So: act on the one verified thing, at standard experiment scale on the SMB self-serve funnel, not broad rollout — exp_86 measured a 30-day window and says nothing about behavior across a full renewal cycle under active competitive pressure, and the churning accounts are existing customers whom an onboarding change does not directly reach. I am proposing the best-evidenced move, not a complete answer to today's churn. Instrument for renewal-cycle retention, not just completion, so this experiment does not become the next confidently-summarized memory with its caveats stripped out. If leadership needs immediate relief for at-risk existing accounts, that should be a separate, explicitly reversible retention action rather than a discount generalized from exp_73.
